name: Sick Cloud
description: A green face mid-retch floating in soft air. 🤢☁️ means something is so disgusting it makes you feel untethered from reality, or that you're dreamily nauseous—caught between two states at once.
meaning: The nausea of 🤢 collides with the dreaminess of ☁️ to create a surreal disgust, as if the thing that repels you has lifted you into a strange, floaty headspace. It reads as 'I am so grossed out I'm not even on solid ground anymore' or 'this is revolting in a way that makes no sense to me.'
examples: just watched him eat mayo straight from the jar 🤢☁️
the way she chews with her mouth open 🤢☁️ im leaving
my ex just posted a thirst trap in his mom's kitchen 🤢☁️
that outfit combo is sending me to another dimension 🤢☁️
he said he prefers his eggs lukewarm 🤢☁️
seoDescription: What does 🤢☁️ mean? Disgust so intense it becomes surreal and disorienting—revulsion that lifts you out of reality into a dreamlike, floating state of bewilderment.

longForm.overview:
🤢☁️ lands when disgust becomes so intense it feels detached from reality. The green face is already visceral—it's the emoji of something truly revolting—but adding the cloud warps it into something dreamlike and disorienting. The combo reads as 'I am so repulsed I've lost my grip on normal space,' which is why it works for both genuine disgust and the exaggerated, dramatic kind.

The two parts work against each other in a way that creates a specific tone: nausea is grounded and physical, clouds are soft and floating. Together they suggest a kind of surreal revulsion, the feeling of being sick in a place that doesn't quite exist. On Twitter and in group chats, 🤢☁️ shows up when someone wants to convey that whatever they just witnessed has fundamentally altered their perception. It's stronger than 🤢 alone because the cloud adds a layer of dislocation—not just disgust, but disgust that has unmoored you.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
🤢☁️ arrives as the reaction to something genuinely off-putting: a weird eating habit, a cringe social media post, a confession that makes no sense. In group chats it lands under a screenshot or a description of something that warrants total revulsion. On Twitter it threads beneath replies to strange takes or bizarre behavior, often paired with 'i'm speechless' energy.

The combo also works as exaggerated reaction to mildly uncomfortable things—a weird outfit choice, an overshare, a dating app bio that doesn't add up. Gen Z especially uses 🤢☁️ to mark the moment when something is so strange or gross that the normal response feels inadequate, and the cloud lifts the disgust into absurdist territory.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Avoid 🤢☁️ in contexts where disgust will read as cruel or personal. Sending it in response to someone's appearance, food preference, or habit risks landing as mockery rather than shared bewilderment. It also misfires in professional settings or serious conversations where you need to express legitimate concern rather than revulsion.

Skip 🤢☁️ when talking to someone who is already feeling vulnerable or defensive. The surreal, dreamlike quality of the combo can read as dismissive or as if you're making fun of them rather than reacting to their behavior. If you want to express genuine disgust without the floating-away vibe, 🤢 alone is sharper and more grounded.
longForm.howToReply:
Mirror 🤢☁️ with your own 🤢☁️ or 🤢 if you want to validate the revulsion and keep the energy going. A simple 'i saw that too' or 'i know' anchors the shared disgust without escalating. If someone sends 🤢☁️ about something you did or said, a soft laugh or acknowledgment ('ok that's fair') defuses the moment better than defensiveness.

If 🤢☁️ lands on your own post or behavior, you can lean into it with self-deprecation or humor rather than explaining yourself. The combo is almost always meant to be funny—even when it's genuine disgust, there's a performative edge. Meeting it with lightness keeps the tone where it belongs.

faqs.question: Is 🤢☁️ actually about being sick or is it about disgust
faqs.answer: It's about disgust that feels so intense it becomes surreal and disorienting. The cloud transforms the nausea from a physical feeling into something dreamlike and untethered, so it reads more as 'I am so repulsed I don't know where I am' than 'my stomach hurts.'

faqs.question: Can you use 🤢☁️ about a person or is that mean
faqs.answer: It lands as mean when aimed at someone's appearance or inherent trait. It works better when directed at someone's choices or behavior—what they posted, what they said, how they acted. The target should feel like a choice they made, not who they are.

faqs.question: What's the difference between 🤢☁️ and just 🤢
faqs.answer: 🤢 alone is sharp and direct disgust. 🤢☁️ adds a floating, dreamlike quality that makes the disgust feel surreal and exaggerated, as if the thing that repels you has knocked you into another dimension. It's more theatrical.

faqs.question: Does 🤢☁️ work in serious conversations
faqs.answer: Not really. The cloud softens the nausea into something absurdist and performative, so it reads as dismissive or flippant in moments that need genuine concern. Save it for reactions to strange or cringe behavior, not for serious problems.

conversationExamples.message: just found out he's been taking meetings in his car with the engine running 🤢☁️
conversationExamples.interpretation: This is someone reporting genuinely bizarre workplace behavior with a mix of bewilderment and revulsion. The sender is not angry—they're trying to process something so strange it doesn't make sense. The right response is agreement or a 'why would he do that' because you're both confused together.

conversationExamples.message: she told me she hasn't washed her sheets in 3 months 🤢☁️ i cant unhear this
conversationExamples.interpretation: A friend shared something gross and the sender is reacting with theatrical disgust. This is playful but also genuinely unsettled. Respond with matching revulsion or a joke about it, not advice—they just need to process the grossness out loud.

conversationExamples.message: he said he thinks pineapple pizza is 'the only correct way' 🤢☁️ we're done
conversationExamples.interpretation: This is exaggerated disgust at a weird opinion, delivered with humor. The sender is not actually ending things over pizza—they're using the combo to say 'this is such a bizarre take it makes me question your judgment.' Reply with laughter or a joke that validates the absurdity.

conversationExamples.message: mom just told me she rewears her jeans without washing them and i need to leave 🤢☁️
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family overshare that's landed wrong. The sender is reacting with revulsion and humor because they didn't want to know this about their parent. Don't defend the behavior—just acknowledge that some information doesn't need to be shared in families.

conversationExamples.message: watched someone order a well-done steak with ketchup and now i understand nothing 🤢☁️
conversationExamples.interpretation: A tweet or post about witnessing something so strange it feels surreal. The sender is performing revulsion for an audience, inviting others to validate that this thing is genuinely odd. Engage with the absurdity—'i'm so sorry you had to see that' or your own version of the disgusting behavior.
